title: Dee Sinks in a Bog

jokes.text: Mac wakes Dennis by pouring a bowl of hot stew directly in his face, then justifies it as a wake-up method
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to wake Dennis up and says 'Breathe in the arousing aromas of this delicious st...' before trailing off
jokes.punchline: He just dumps the stew on Dennis's face — 'that's a whole bowl of stew you took right in the grill. See? It does wake people up.'
jokes.explanation: Perfect cold-open energy. Mac's smug self-satisfaction — 'See? It does wake people up' — is classic character comedy. The trailing off before the act of violence gives it great structure. Very on-brand for the gang's casual cruelty toward each other.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: of this delicious st... Ah, screw it.

jokes.text: Dee looks at Dennis's hospital neck and asks 'Did they reattach it? Left the skin pretty loose, I see.'
jokes.setup: Dennis wakes up in the hospital asking why he's there. Dee is visiting.
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately insults his neck skin rather than showing any concern for her hospitalized brother.
jokes.explanation: Encapsulates the sibling dynamic perfectly. 'Left the skin pretty loose, I see' is an unusually specific and vicious insult. The complete absence of concern for her hospitalized brother is pure Dee-as-terrible-person character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What the hell was that? That's hot as shit.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, that's a whole bowl of stew you took right in the grill.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I'm starting to think I might have had COVID.' Dee: 'Oh, yeah? You think?'
jokes.setup: Dennis had a 105-degree fever, hallucinations, was too weak to lift an ax, collapsed, and shit himself in a castle.
jokes.punchline: He delivers the COVID self-diagnosis as a tentative revelation, as if it's a novel insight. Dee's 'Oh yeah? You think?' drips with contempt.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis obliviousness — his self-aggrandizement means he can't even acknowledge obvious illness without framing it as a considered conclusion. Dee's reaction is perfectly calibrated contempt. COVID reference grounds the absurdist castle storyline in reality.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: And why is your head still on? Did they reattach it? Left the skin pretty loose, I see.

jokes.text: Doctor asks 'How are we feeling?' Dennis lists: 'outraged, violated, disgusted at the looseness of my sister's neck, covered in stew, dragged from my castle to a dingy hospital where I'm about to be saddled with an enormous bill.'
jokes.setup: Doctor professionally asks 'how are we feeling' expecting a medical answer.
jokes.punchline: Dennis launches into a tirade of narcissistic grievances in ascending order of pettiness, culminating in the neck insult callback and financial complaint.
jokes.explanation: This is Dennis at his most Dennis. The list structure is brilliantly ordered: 'outraged, violated' sounds medical, then 'disgusted at the looseness of my sister's neck' is a perfectly absurd vanity pivot, then 'covered in stew' is matter-of-fact, then the financial complaint. It escalates through self-pity into pure narcissism. The callback to the neck insult shows the writers' precision — Dennis internalized his sister's dig and is now truly worried about his neck. Character integration is as high as it gets.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You did collapse and shit yourself and stink up the whole castle.

jokes.text: Dennis learns Ireland has free public healthcare: 'Oh, well, then that'll be fine... Well, then maybe I ought to get my neck done.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is mid-complaint about an enormous hospital bill.
jokes.punchline: Told it's free, he instantly pivots to exploiting it for cosmetic neck surgery — the neck insult from Dee has genuinely lodged in his vanity.
jokes.explanation: This is the best payoff of the episode's first act. Three jokes have been building to this: Dee's neck insult, Dennis's list of grievances including the neck, and now Dennis weaponizing Ireland's healthcare system for vanity surgery. The misdirection is perfect — his complaint about bills is instantly abandoned when the system benefits him. 'Maybe I ought to get my neck done' is quotable and devastatingly in-character. The callback architecture is tight and rewarding.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, then maybe I ought to get my neck done.

jokes.text: Dee, alone in a hospital corridor, says to herself: 'Looks like mama's about to have a little of the old luck of the Irish.'
jokes.setup: The Irish doctor agreed to drinks with Dee. She walks away from the room.
jokes.punchline: Dee's self-congratulatory talking-to-herself, calling herself 'mama' while using a hacky Irish phrase, is pure deluded Dee energy.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specificity of Dee's self-delusion. 'Mama' is especially cringeworthy. It's a compact character beat that efficiently establishes her storyline while being funny on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah? Have you heard the one about the hot Irish doctor who has a fling with the hilarious American tourist?

jokes.text: Frank enters the hospital like Frankenstein. Dennis: 'Oh, Christ. Frankenstein in the house.'
jokes.setup: The hospital scene is wrapping up with sibling tension.
jokes.punchline: Frank barges in, apparently moving in an odd, lumbering way that prompts Dennis's 'Frankenstein in the house' remark — a name-pun on Frank's name that also describes his manner of entry.
jokes.explanation: A quick visual/wordplay gag on Frank's name and presumably his entrance. Functional but not exceptional — relies on a pretty obvious wordplay and physical entrance gag.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Looks like mama's about to have a little of the old luck of the Irish.

jokes.text: Frank tries to get Dennis to kiss him — 'Give your daddy a kiss' — and Dennis physically recoils: 'Get your lips away from me, Frank.'
jokes.setup: Frank wants a kiss to perform fatherly affection.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's visceral, specific 'Get your lips away from me, Frank' — not 'no' or 'stop it' but specifically about the lips — implies Frank's approach is physically threatening.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'your lips' makes this more effective than a generic refusal. Frank's physical approach to affection being inherently threatening is a consistent character trait that the show mines well.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, Christ! Frankenstein in the house.

jokes.text: Dennis agrees to help Frank humiliate Shelley only if 'we can incorporate the castle into it in some way.'
jokes.setup: Frank wants to humiliate Charlie's new dad. Dee is ranting about her ruined trip.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's singular condition for participation isn't about family loyalty or even fun — it's purely about using the castle. His obsession with the castle is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis priority inversion — he doesn't care about family drama but is passionate about castle utility. 'Incorporate the castle into it in some way' is perfectly Dennis: even his schemes require an aesthetic framework.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, no! God. Get your lips away from me, Frank.

jokes.text: Dee's explosive rant about her ruined trip ending with her going to gather peat moss to burn to cover the shit smell Dennis left in the castle, then: 'Do not be here when I get back.' Frank and Dennis: 'Cool.'
jokes.setup: Dee launches into an extended rant about how her trip has been ruined.
jokes.punchline: After a dramatic tirade, her plan is to go gather peat in a bog. Frank and Dennis's flat 'Cool' completely deflates her outrage.
jokes.explanation: The 'Cool' reaction beat from both Dennis and Frank is perfectly timed. The joke is that Dee's grand declaration resolves to 'going to a bog to get peat' — an inherently undignified errand — and no one cares. The indifference punctures her drama beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Like, you know, father-son thing. I mean, you know, it's one of the strongest bonds there is. Come on. Give me a kiss.

jokes.text: Frank and Dennis alone together, awkwardly acknowledging they 'usually have a buffer.'
jokes.setup: Dee has stormed off. It's just Frank and Dennis.
jokes.punchline: Frank admits it's 'a little odd being one on one' — they need a third person to function as a group. The acknowledgment is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: A self-aware meta-observation about the gang's group dynamics that rings true. These characters' relationships are fundamentally mediated through the group — one-on-one they have nothing. The long pause implied by the transcript before Frank speaks is part of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Charlie's got a new dad. A-a new dad? Weird. Yeah. I want to humiliate the jerk. I want to send his Irish ass packing.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He's jealous.

jokes.text: Mac explains his call to the priesthood: 'When God took away my Irish identity and made me Dutch to smite me for the urges that He gave me when I made the original sin of being born.'
jokes.setup: An Irish priest asks Mac when he felt the call to become a priest.
jokes.punchline: Mac delivers a theologically incoherent, self-contradictory statement that blames God for his identity, his urges, and his very birth — all as evidence of divine punishment.
jokes.explanation: Mac's tortured relationship with God and his sexuality is one of the show's richest running threads. This line captures it with unusual precision: 'the original sin of being born' is a remarkable piece of Mac-logic, suggesting he holds himself responsible for his own existence. The Dutch identity reference ties to the season's arc. Character integration is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm going to go down to the bog, I'm going to gather peat moss to burn it to try and get rid of the shit smell that Dennis stunk up the castle with.

jokes.text: Mac's Bible history: 'Noah made the ark, and he saved himself but no women, which was really cool. Not sure how he made more people after that, though. Could've been another rib situation.'
jokes.setup: Mac is defending his view of a smiting God by citing Noah's Ark.
jokes.punchline: Mac either doesn't know or doesn't care that Noah saved his family (including women), and his nonchalant 'rib situation' as a reproductive solution reveals spectacular Biblical ignorance wrapped in breezy confidence.
jokes.explanation: 'Could've been another rib situation' is a genuinely excellent piece of comedy writing — it's specific, absurd, delivered with Mac's characteristic breezy confidence in his own nonsense. The idea that Mac finds an all-male ark 'really cool' and then waves away the reproduction problem with a casual theological hand-wave is both funny and revealing of his character. High quotability.

dialogue.line: She's... Bent out of shape.

jokes.text: Mac's Indiana Jones/Ark of the Covenant confusion: 'Then a bunch of people looked at it. He didn't like that, so he blasted them. Remember, the Nazis got their faces all melted off, and the guy with the whip and the hat, he was cool.'
jokes.setup: Mac is continuing his Bible history, moving from Noah to the Ark of the Covenant.
jokes.punchline: Mac has completely merged Raiders of the Lost Ark with the Bible, treating Indiana Jones as a Biblical figure ('the guy with the whip and the hat') and movie events as Scripture.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Mac has not only confused Indiana Jones with the Bible but treats the movie's events as the actual canonical scripture. 'The guy with the whip and the hat, he was cool' is a perfect encapsulation of Mac's theology — reverence for masculine cool is his actual religion. The priest's 'I think you've mixed that story up with Indiana Jones' is a beautifully understated correction. This is exceptionally well-crafted character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, when God took away my Irish identity and made me Dutch to smite me for the urges that He gave me when I made the original sin of being born.

jokes.text: Mac's response after being told the Ark of the Covenant story is Indiana Jones: 'What's the lesson of the last one? Don't look at my shit?'
jokes.setup: The priest explains that Bible stories are metaphors with lessons.
jokes.punchline: Mac applies this pedagogical framework to Indiana Jones and arrives at 'Don't look at my shit?' as the film's moral lesson — attributing the face-melting to a jealous God's privacy preferences.
jokes.explanation: This might be the single most quotable line in the episode. Mac's reduction of divine wrath — and by extension the entire Indiana Jones climax — to 'Don't look at my shit?' is shockingly economical and funny. It captures his theology perfectly: God is a masculine authority figure with territorial instincts, like a mob boss. The vulgarity of 'shit' in a theological discussion is perfectly calibrated. High craft, high impact, extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Remember? Then-then-then Noah made that ark, and he saved himself but no women, which was really cool. Not sure how he made more people after that, though. Could've been another rib situation.

jokes.text: The priest tells Mac 'Our God is a merciful God. One that loves us for exactly who we are. Otherwise, why would He have made us that way in the first place?' — clearly implying acceptance of gay identity.
jokes.setup: Mac has laid out his tortured theology. The priest seems to be offering theological acceptance.
jokes.punchline: The audience understands this is about Mac's gay identity, but the punchline is withheld — we're watching Mac receive genuine affirmation that is about to be complicated.
jokes.explanation: This is structural comedy — the joke is in the expectation it sets up and what it's about to invert. Scored moderately as a standalone joke; it's doing setup work for the larger payoff at 10:25 and 14:37.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Either way, then God made the Ark of the Covenant where he promised to never, ever do it again. Then a bunch of people looked at it. He didn't like that, so he blasted them, too. Remember, the Nazis got their faces all melted off, and the-the guy with the whip and the hat, he was cool.

jokes.text: Mac learns Kelly family members who died of plague, violence, and one who 'was attacked by the village loon, became a loon himself. He died from eating rocks, which he thought were eggs.' Mac: 'Oof. Yeah, I've made that mistake, yeah.'
jokes.setup: The priest recounts grim Kelly family history at a graveyard.
jokes.punchline: Mac casually identifies with dying from eating rocks, suggesting this is a relatable error for him specifically.
jokes.explanation: 'Yeah, I've made that mistake, yeah' — the double 'yeah' makes this. Mac's breezy admission that he has personally confused rocks with eggs is a perfect non sequitur that's also completely believable for the character. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Remember, the Nazis got their faces all melted off, and the-the guy with the whip and the hat, he was cool.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Oof. Yeah, I've made that mistake, yeah.' — responding to Michael Kelly dying from eating rocks he thought were eggs
jokes.setup: Shelley solemnly describes an ancestor dying from eating rocks he thought were eggs
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually identifies with this, implying he has also eaten rocks believing them to be eggs — a perfect Charlie revelation delivered with no emphasis
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a candidate for one of the best Charlie lines of the season. The structure is flawless: Shelley's earnest tragic recounting is completely upended by Charlie's casual 'Oof. Yeah, I've made that mistake, yeah.' It works on two levels simultaneously: as a character joke (of course Charlie has eaten rocks thinking they were eggs) and as a darkness joke (we now know something about Charlie that is both funny and deeply concerning). The economy is perfect — the 'yeah...yeah' at the end adds the specific Charlie rhythm. High quotability, high rewatch.

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: I think you've mixed that story up with Indiana Jones.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh. I did?

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: Yeah, but listen...

jokes.text: Mac asks about the women. Priest: 'Oh, the women are thrown from a cliff as well. Mostly alive. Just to see if they can fly, as they're presumed to be witches.'
jokes.setup: Mac asks if women get the same honor as the men.
jokes.punchline: 'Mostly alive' — the casual qualifier on 'alive' is the joke. Then the witch-flying test adds Medieval absurdism delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: 'Mostly alive' is a masterpiece of comic economy — two words that imply a spectrum of aliveness for the women being thrown, without any additional explanation needed. The witch-test framing takes a dark premise and frames it with officious reasonableness. The priest's matter-of-fact delivery makes this land harder. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What's the lesson of the last one? Don't look at my shit?

jokes.text: The priest's description of the banshee: 'If you ever see a gruesome woman covered in filth with long, stringy hair, who's horribly shrieking in the night, the end is near.'
jokes.setup: The priest is explaining Irish folklore about the women's spirits becoming banshees.
jokes.punchline: The banshee description is an exact description of Dee — who is currently at the bog at night, covered in bog mud, struggling and shrieking. This is dramatic irony the audience will realize when cut to Dee.
jokes.explanation: Structurally this is excellent writing. The priest's folklore speech about banshees cuts directly to Dee stuck in a bog, covered in filth, shrieking — she IS the banshee. The comedic architecture is tight: we get the description, then the visual confirmation, and later characters literally mistake Dee for a banshee. The setup here is doing heavy lifting for payoffs across the whole episode. High structure score.

dialogue.speaker: Shelley
dialogue.line: And Michael Kelly. He was attacked by the village loon, became a loon himself. He died from eating rocks, which he thought were eggs.

jokes.text: Cut to Dee in the bog at night, confused about peat: 'I mean, how am I supposed to know what peat is? What am I, a botanist?'
jokes.setup: Dee went to the bog to gather peat moss. It's dark.
jokes.punchline: 'What am I, a botanist?' — Dee's indignant defense against the expectation that she should know basic things. Classic Dee self-pity.
jokes.explanation: A quick, competent character beat. 'What am I, a botanist?' is a perfectly Dee complaint — she's annoyed at her own incompetence and externally blaming the expectation. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oof. Yeah, I've made that mistake, yeah.

jokes.text: Dee, in the bog at night, tries to take a selfie. She notices the bad angle, tries moving back — and falls further into the bog.
jokes.setup: Dee is alone in a dark bog, ostensibly gathering peat, but instead she's preening for a selfie after Dennis's comments about her neck.
jokes.punchline: Her attempt to get a better angle on her neck/appearance leads to stepping backward into the bog. Vanity causes the disaster.
jokes.explanation: The thematic coherence here is excellent — Dennis's neck comments have now infected Dee, who is inspecting her own neck in a bog at night. Her vanity literally causes her to sink. This is tight structural writing where character flaws have physical consequences. The callback to the neck joke runs through the whole episode.

dialogue.line: Oh, the women are thrown from a cliff as well. Mostly alive. Just to see if they can fly, as they're presumed to be witches.

jokes.text: Dennis's neck insecurity triggers Dee to examine her own neck in her phone camera, leading her to sink deeper
jokes.setup: Dee is already sinking in a bog
jokes.punchline: Dennis's neck comments have planted enough insecurity that Dee is now inspecting her own neck on her phone camera while sinking — vanity literally causing her death
jokes.explanation: Smart callback payoff to the neck running gag. Dee being distracted by neck-checking while sinking is a perfect visual articulation of the show's thesis: these people's vanity is literally killing them. The rewatch bonus is for catching the thematic symmetry with Dennis's neck reveal.

dialogue.line: If you ever see a gruesome woman covered in filth with long, stringy hair, who's horribly shrieking in the night, the end is near.

jokes.text: Dennis and Frank discuss the humiliation plan. Frank: 'Wait a minute. The old turd in the soup trick.' Dennis: 'We're not putting a turd in someone's soup, Frank, okay? Can we be a little more sophisticated than that?'
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining a sophisticated castle-based humiliation scheme.
jokes.punchline: Frank's first instinct is immediately 'turd in the soup' — his baseline for humiliation pranks. Dennis's exasperated 'Can we be a little more sophisticated?' while plotting to pour boiling oil on a man is a perfect irony.
jokes.explanation: Frank's immediate 'turd in the soup trick' as a named, established prank technique is a great character detail — he has a whole repertoire of excrement-based pranks. Dennis's appeal to sophistication while planning something arguably worse is excellent dramatic irony. Character integration is very high.

dialogue.line: The women roam the land as terrible hags and banshees whose wailing warns of impending death.

jokes.text: Dennis explains the castle's 'murder hole.' Frank: 'Is that like a glory hole?' Dennis: 'A predecessor to the glory hole, perhaps. It's a discreet opening concealed in plain sight, except instead of for sex, it's used for murder.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining the castle's architectural features for their scheme.
jokes.punchline: Frank's completely sincere glory hole association, and Dennis's measured etymological response — 'a predecessor to the glory hole, perhaps' — treats the murder/sex comparison as a reasonable historical progression.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely excellent joke. 'A predecessor to the glory hole, perhaps' is a remarkable line — Dennis treats this as a plausible architectural history without irony. The parallel construction ('discreet opening concealed in plain sight, except instead of for sex, it's used for murder') is tight and funny. Frank's earnest question is what makes it land — he has no shame and no filter. High quotability and craft.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I mean, how am I supposed to know what peat is? What am I, a botanist?

jokes.text: Frank describes pouring boiling oil from the murder hole: 'I'm not gonna kill him or anything, but it's got to be hot enough to be annoying as shit.' Dennis: 'You know what I mean?' Frank: 'Yeah. Burn him.'
jokes.setup: Frank is enthusiastically planning to pour boiling oil on Shelley.
jokes.punchline: Frank's self-imposed ethical limit is 'hot enough to be annoying' — murder is off the table, but severe burns are acceptable. His casual 'burn him' is a perfect understatement of the violence being planned.
jokes.explanation: 'Not gonna kill him, but hot enough to be annoying as shit' is a great Frank line — the ethical floor being 'not murder' while planning boiling oil pours is exactly his moral register. 'Yeah. Burn him.' as the summary is good deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Hey-o. I'll burn you. Be like lighting a match. That works.

jokes.text: Dennis explains he wants to cut out eyeholes in a painting to watch from the secret passageway: 'That's something I've always wanted to do, and it fully takes advantage of the castle.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is describing the castle's secret passageway as a surveillance position.
jokes.punchline: His admission that cutting eyeholes in a portrait painting is a lifelong dream — and his framing of it as 'taking advantage of the castle' — reveals that Dennis has had a whole fantasy life about castle-based espionage.
jokes.explanation: 'That's something I've always wanted to do' applied to portrait eyeholes is excellent Dennis character writing. His castle obsession manifesting as a bucket list of medieval spying activities is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Dennis got me all worked up about my neck.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'It also happens to be the castle's preference for how this is all gonna go down.' Frank: 'Oh, right.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining the castle-based plan.
jokes.punchline: Dennis refers to the castle as having active 'preferences' for how events unfold, and Frank accepts this completely without question.
jokes.explanation: Dennis treating the castle as a sentient being with preferences is a great running absurdist thread. Frank's 'Oh, right' — total acceptance — is the punchline. No elaboration needed from either character. The joke trusts the audience.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, shit, I'm sinking.

jokes.text: Dennis credits his diabolical scheming to Frank's neglect and misdeeds: 'I suppose all of your years of neglect and misdeeds have allowed me to harness the darkness inside me and to unleash it without conscience, so... thanks for making me the man I am today, Frank.'
jokes.setup: Frank compliments Dennis's plan as 'diabolical.'
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a sincere-sounding expression of gratitude to Frank for the abuse/neglect that made him a sociopath. It's framed as a heartwarming father-son moment.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character moments. Dennis thanking Frank for his abuse because it enabled his sociopathy is dark and funny, but also genuinely touching in the context of this show — it IS a real father-son bond, just a horrifying one. 'Without conscience' is key: Dennis is proud of the absence of conscience. Character integration is as high as it gets for this show.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Wait a minute. The old turd in the soup trick.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I suppose all of your years of neglect and misdeeds have allowed me to harness the darkness inside me and to unleash it without conscience, so... thanks for making me the man I am today, Frank.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dennis are having an unexpected father-son moment of genuine connection
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a heartfelt thanks-to-dad speech, except the gift his father gave him is the capacity for conscienceless evil
jokes.explanation: Genuinely well-crafted dark comedy. The speech hits every beat of a sincere father-son gratitude moment — 'made me the man I am today' — while the content is Dennis thanking Frank for psychologically breaking him into a sociopath. The 'so...' pause before 'thanks' is perfect. It earns its dark laugh because the character work is so deep. Rewatch bonus for the emotional sincerity underneath the horror.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Is that like a-a glory hole? A predecessor to the glory hole, perhaps.

jokes.text: Frank and Dennis share an awkward hug/pat. Dennis: 'Was that okay to do?' Frank: 'Yeah, it was nice.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just thanked Frank for making him a monster. The scene has accidentally become tender.
jokes.punchline: The mutual uncertainty about whether a hug between them is acceptable — 'Was that okay to do?' — is painfully funny given these characters don't have normal emotional reflexes.
jokes.explanation: The economy here is extraordinary — two short lines doing enormous emotional and comedic work. These characters are so emotionally stunted that a hug requires consent negotiation. 'Yeah, it was nice' from Frank is quietly devastating. This is the show at its best: mining genuine character pathos for comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It also happens to be the castle's preference for how this is all gonna go down.

jokes.text: Mac: 'So, you're telling me the whole Cain and Abel thing didn't actually happen?' Priest: 'Metaphor.' Mac: 'This is all so confusing.'
jokes.setup: The priest has been explaining that Bible stories are metaphors.
jokes.punchline: Mac is genuinely struggling with the metaphor concept, as if each new application of it is a fresh confusion rather than a pattern he can apply.
jokes.explanation: A functional running gag on Mac's Biblical literalism. The single-word answer 'Metaphor' from the priest is nicely timed. Mac's 'This is all so confusing' is appropriately exhausted. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I suppose all of your years of neglect and misdeeds have allowed me to harness the darkness inside me and to unleash it without conscience, so... Yeah, perhaps I owe you a... thanks for making me the man I am today, Frank. Thank you.

jokes.text: Mac does a 'That's what he said' and the priest shushes him. Mac: 'Sorry.'
jokes.setup: The priest just did 'That's what he said' and apologized.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately does the same joke and gets shushed — implying Mac can't help himself either, linking their shared lack of self-control.
jokes.explanation: The doubling of the joke with Mac doing it immediately after works as a beat — it bonds them through their shared inability to resist the punchline. Competent escalation of the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: all of your years of neglect and misdeeds have allowed me to harness the darkness inside me

jokes.text: The Waitress appears in the bog at night carrying a toiletry bag. Dee: 'What the hell are you doing out here with a toiletry bag?'
jokes.setup: Dee is stuck in a bog at night, screaming for help.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress is her rescuer — also mysteriously in the bog at night, also for a mundane grooming reason.
jokes.explanation: The random appearance of the Waitress in an Irish bog is absurdly funny. The show doesn't explain it and doesn't need to. The parallel of both women being in a bog at night for vanity-adjacent reasons is a nice thematic echo.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There. Was that okay to do?

jokes.text: Dee: 'I also don't want to die, but, either way, could you just give me a big tug?' — presenting 'not dying' as a secondary motivation after the date
jokes.setup: Dee is explaining to the Waitress why she needs to get out of the bog
jokes.punchline: She lists her hot doctor date as the primary reason to escape, with 'I also don't want to die' as a casual afterthought
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dee priorities joke. The structure of listing the date before not dying is excellent, and 'either way' as the bridge is casual genius — it treats the two motivations as equally viable, leaving the door open for a world where she dies but still makes the date. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's what he said. That's-that's really good. Thank you. I'm sorry. It just slipped out. That's what he said.

jokes.text: Dee mentions wanting to get out for her hot Irish doctor date. Waitress: 'Is he meeting you here, or...?'
jokes.setup: Dee explains she has a date with a hot doctor tonight.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress drily asks if the doctor is coming to the bog — implying this is a plausible outcome for Dee's romantic life.
jokes.explanation: 'Is he meeting you here, or...?' is excellent deadpan. The trailing 'or' is doing a lot of work — it implies Dee's circumstances are so perpetually unfortunate that bog-dates are on the table. Economy is near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's-that's really good. Thank you. I'm sorry. It just slipped out. That's what he said.

jokes.text: The Waitress does 'Psych!' — pretending to grab Dee's hand then pulling back — multiple times.
jokes.setup: The Waitress is about to rescue Dee from the bog.
jokes.punchline: Instead of helping, she does multiple rounds of 'Psych!' — holding out her hand then pulling away while Dee continues sinking.
jokes.explanation: The Waitress torturing Dee while she sinks is excellent cringe-escalation. The show's dynamic of everyone treating Dee as the lowest status member of any group is well-deployed here. The escalation across three 'psychs' builds nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Psych! Your face. I'm kidding. No, I got you. Psych!

jokes.text: Dee: 'Nobody does "psych" anymore. It's kind of dumb.' Waitress: 'Oh, do they not?' — then does Psych again.
jokes.setup: Dee criticizes the Waitress for using 'Psych' — an outdated expression.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress's 'Oh, do they not?' is completely flat — she doesn't care at all — and immediately does it again. Dee's critique has zero effect.
jokes.explanation: The Waitress's total indifference to Dee's criticism — followed by immediate repetition — is good character work. Dee's attempt to regain dignity by critiquing the joke format while sinking in a bog is appropriately pathetic.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Oh, do they not? Nah, it's not funny, it's dumb.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I feel like it's classic.

jokes.text: Waitress says she'll save Dee if Dee says her name. Dee struggles to remember it. The Waitress: 'No, no. You got it a while back. It's just... I'm really enjoying watching you struggle.'
jokes.setup: The Waitress offers to save Dee's life in exchange for Dee saying her name — a name Dee doesn't know, reinforcing the long-running joke that none of the gang has ever learned the Waitress's name.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress admits she already knows Dee got it right — she's just withholding rescue to watch Dee suffer. Active sadism dressed as a game.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and one of the best payoffs of a long-running series gag. The Waitress leveraging a life-or-death situation to extract her own name from Dee is wickedly funny on its own. But the revelation — 'You got it a while back, I'm just really enjoying watching you struggle' — takes it to another level entirely. It recontextualizes the whole scene: the Waitress is not just withholding rescue, she is actively prolonging Dee's suffering for personal entertainment while Dee sinks. This is dark comedy at its sharpest: the structure is perfect, the character integration is total (this ONLY works with these two specific characters and their history), and it earns its darkness completely.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Just say my name. What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, o... kay, yeah. Just, just give me a second.

jokes.text: Dee calls the Waitress a 'drunk bitch.'
jokes.setup: Dee realizes the Waitress has been holding out on her.
jokes.punchline: 'Drunk bitch' — Dee's go-to escalation. The abrupt, unfiltered insult from a sinking woman is a release valve after the cringe buildup.
jokes.explanation: It's not clever writing, but it's perfectly in character for Dee and functions as a beat release. The simplicity is the joke — after the elaborate Psych game and name negotiation, Dee falls back on her baseline insult mode.

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: And we'll never, ever leave each other alone in the room with the wee lads. Yes, and I also think... Wait, what? Or the wee lasses, whatever you're into.

jokes.text: Mac's coming-out moment: 'Yeah, I'm gay. What are you talking about?' — after the priest's speech turns out to be about covering up abuse.
jokes.setup: The priest and Mac have been bonding over shared 'urges' (implied to be gay identity). The priest then reveals the Church's actual plan: transfer to a new parish, silence the family, money changes hands.
jokes.punchline: Mac, realizing the priest means something else entirely, clarifies with exasperation: 'Yeah, I'm gay. What are you talking about?' — a rare moment of Mac being the clearer thinker in a conversation.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode, possibly the series. The setup is a masterpiece of layered misdirection: (1) The priest seems to be accepting Mac's gay identity with warmth. (2) Then he reveals they 'must never act on those urges.' (3) Then his description of the Church's resolution system — new parish, money, 'no harm no foul' — reveals he's describing institutional child abuse cover-up protocols, not celibacy. (4) Mac, whose threshold for subtext is usually zero, cuts through it instantly: 'Yeah, I'm gay. What are you talking about?' Mac's clarification is both funny and genuinely principled — he's distinguishing between gay adult relationships and what the priest is actually describing. The structure is perfect, character integration is total (this joke only works because of Mac's entire arc), and the earned-vs-cheap score is high because the dark subject matter is handled with precision rather than shock value.

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: And, of course, you know, if you do slip up, you'll go to a new parish, they sort the family out, have some chats, perhaps some money changes hands, perhaps not. No harm, no foul.

jokes.text: Frank calls Shelley 'Shirley' multiple times. Charlie corrects him: 'Frank, his name is Shelley.' Frank: 'Shirley, let me take your coat.' Shelley: 'I'm not wearing a coat.'
jokes.setup: Frank is hosting a dinner to humiliate Charlie's new Irish dad Shelley.
jokes.punchline: Frank deliberately or incompetently calls Shelley 'Shirley' throughout — a feminizing insult — and then tries to take a coat Shelley isn't wearing.
jokes.explanation: The 'Shirley' mispronunciation is an old but effective belittlement technique from Frank. The 'coat' bit — trying to perform a hosting ritual for a coat that doesn't exist — is a good added absurdist beat. Competent Frank-being-awful comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm gay. What are you talking about? Oh... No. I'm gay. That's it. I'm a gay man. I'm a gay man who has trouble controlling his urges with other gay adult men, and that's the end of it.

jokes.text: Charlie explains the coat is 'buttoned to his pants in traditional Irish style.' Shelley: 'I'm not wearing a coat.'
jokes.setup: Frank tries to take Shelley's coat.
jokes.punchline: Charlie invents a 'traditional Irish style' where coats are buttoned to pants — absolute nonsense — and Shelley patiently clarifies he's simply not wearing a coat.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's earnest invention of Irish tradition is very funny. 'Buttoned to his pants in traditional Irish style' has no basis in reality, delivered with complete sincerity. Shelley's flat correction — 'I'm not wearing a coat' — is perfect straight-man work. Good character integration for Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Swim goggles? Yeah, they're good ones, too. They'll protect your eyes from any chlorine or oils or any other hot liquid that might come in contact with your face.

jokes.text: Frank: 'I think cheese should be sprayed out of a can, but to each his own.'
jokes.setup: Charlie and Shelley present homemade cheese as a gift.
jokes.punchline: Frank's considered opinion on cheese — 'sprayed out of a can' — delivered as a reasonable preference with dignified magnanimity ('but to each his own').
jokes.explanation: Very Frank. The specific preference for spray cheese — expressed with the magnanimous 'but to each his own' — is perfect character voice. Frank's complete sincerity about deeply lowbrow preferences, delivered with dignified authority, is a reliable comedy engine.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Are the meatballs turds?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What? No, no, they're homemade meatballs.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Oh, yeah? Well, that can be very blinding. But I'm sure, by the end of the evening, we'll all be seeing clear.'
jokes.setup: Charlie says Shelley has 'opened his eyes to a whole new world.'
jokes.punchline: Frank's response is ominous foreshadowing — 'seeing clear' refers to the boiling-oil plan — but disguised as a platitude. He's telegraphing the murder hole scheme to the audience.
jokes.explanation: A functional dramatic irony beat. 'By the end of the evening we'll all be seeing clear' is an obvious foreshadow of the boiling oil on Shelley's eyes, picked up by both Charlie and Shelley: 'I don't like how you said that.' Rewatch value because it's a clear plant.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I knew it! I knew it, Frank! You're not trying to bring us closer together, you're trying to drive us apart!

jokes.text: Frank's toast: 'It's been a very trying time with Charlie finding his biological father, who abandoned him when he was a child, by the way. Not judging, just the facts.'
jokes.setup: Frank is welcoming everyone to dinner.
jokes.punchline: 'Not judging, just the facts' — the classic passive-aggressive move of issuing a devastating character indictment while disclaiming judgment. The specificity ('who abandoned him when he was a child') in a dinner toast is wickedly inappropriate.
jokes.explanation: 'Not judging, just the facts' as a tonal pivot after a targeted insult in a dinner toast is a great Frank move. It's the passive-aggressive disclaimer that makes the attack more devastating. Solid character writing with good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not coming back to Philly, Frank!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I think there's another man in this room. Never mind him.
What'd you say, Charlie?

jokes.text: Frank gives Shelley swim goggles as a gift 'to protect your eyes from any chlorine or oils or any other hot liquid that might come in contact with your face.'
jokes.setup: Frank announces gifts for everyone. Shelley gets goggles.
jokes.punchline: Frank's gift is explicitly designed for the boiling oil attack — described in terms that make it obvious to the audience and gradually to Shelley — while being framed as genuine hospitality.
jokes.explanation: Frank giving Shelley eye protection for the attack he's about to execute is deliciously dark. The list — 'chlorine or oils or any other hot liquid' — is clearly Frank running through his options. Shelley's 'that's very kind of you, Frank' while not yet realizing is good dramatic irony. Rewatch value because on second viewing you catch exactly how specific Frank is being.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Not eat a poopy.

jokes.text: Charlie asks why there's no present for him. Frank: 'No, no. Just the one gift, just for Shelley.' Then tells everyone to eat up.
jokes.setup: Frank has given only Shelley a gift.
jokes.punchline: Frank's flat refusal to acknowledge Charlie's question — 'Just the one gift, just for Shelley' — while pivoting to 'eat up' has the energy of someone managing a crime scene.
jokes.explanation: Functional beat. Frank's dismissal of Charlie while focusing his evil on Shelley shows his tunnel vision. The 'eat up' pivot is appropriately suspicious.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You drunk bitch!

jokes.text: Charlie finds 'meatballs' in the soup. Dennis's voice from behind the wall: 'Didn't put any goddamn meatballs in that soup.' Then: 'Do you hear something?' Frank: 'Oh, it's probably your stomach grumbling from hunger.'
jokes.setup: Frank announces there are special meatballs in Shelley's soup.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's muffled voice from behind the painting reveals there are no actual meatballs — implying they're something else entirely. Frank covers it with a transparently absurd explanation.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the 'turd in the soup' setup from earlier. Dennis's disembodied voice from behind the painting is both a callback to the spy scheme and the reveal that something is wrong with the meatballs. Frank's cover — 'your stomach grumbling' — is a perfect non-sequitur that doesn't actually address the voice at all. The structure is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You drunk bitch!

jokes.text: Charlie: 'Are the meatballs turds?' Frank: 'What? No, no, they're homemade meatballs.'
jokes.setup: Everyone suspects the meatballs aren't meatballs.
jokes.punchline: Charlie asks the direct question with zero ceremony: 'Are the meatballs turds?' Frank's indignant denial while insisting they're 'homemade' — which somehow makes it more suspicious — is perfect.
jokes.explanation: 'Are the meatballs turds?' is a great Charlie line — perfectly direct, no euphemism, treating this as a reasonable question that simply needs an answer. Frank's 'they're homemade meatballs' as a rebuttal is somehow worse — it implies he made them himself, which doesn't preclude the turd hypothesis. High economy, very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You're doing it. No, you're pulling me in. Yes. No, no, no, no. No, no, no, no. Thank you! It's working. You're doing it. You're pushing me under.

jokes.text: The standoff: Frank, to prove the meatballs aren't turds, must eat one himself. He slowly pulls one out with a spoon and eats it. Long pause. 'Delicious.'
jokes.setup: Frank has claimed the meatballs are fine. Charlie/Shelley demand he eat one.
jokes.punchline: Frank eats the meatball — the long pause before 'Delicious' is the joke. Whether he's eating a turd or just a meatball, his willingness to eat it and declare it delicious is equally horrifying.
jokes.explanation: The long silence before 'Delicious' is extraordinary comic timing. Frank eating the meatball — with no hesitation once challenged — and pronouncing it delicious is a masterclass in character-integrated cringe comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) if it's a turd, Frank ate a turd. (2) if it's not a turd, Frank has committed to eating whatever it is with zero dignity. (3) Frank's 'Delicious' completely fails to prove anything because he would eat a turd and call it delicious. The ambiguity IS the joke. High structure, extraordinary character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Oh, no, I'm not gonna do that 'cause I got a date, but I'll come back after my date. Thank you so much.

jokes.text: Charlie exposes Frank: 'You're not trying to bring us closer together, you're trying to drive us apart! I knew you couldn't host a dinner without a motive.'
jokes.setup: Frank has been pretending the dinner is a peace offering.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's 'You just can't do it' — his diagnosis that Frank is physically incapable of hosting an innocent dinner — is an absurdist character observation delivered with genuine exasperation.
jokes.explanation: 'You just can't do it' as a character diagnosis is a good beat. Charlie's lucidity in this moment — accurately reading Frank's scheme — is funnier because Charlie is usually the least aware character.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What is that? Are you seeing that? What was that?

dialogue.speaker: Shelley
dialogue.line: A banshee.

jokes.text: Charlie announces he's not coming back to Philadelphia — he's staying in Ireland with Shelley. Frank: 'I want to humiliate the jerk' — now sitting across from someone he just failed to humiliate.
jokes.setup: Frank's scheme to expose and humiliate Shelley has failed spectacularly.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's declaration to stay in Ireland is the emotional escalation — but the comedy is in Frank having eaten a possible turd to prove loyalty to Charlie, and Charlie is leaving anyway.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'turd soup dinner' to 'Charlie is leaving Philadelphia forever' is a good structural turn. Frank's manipulation backfiring completely — and doing so after he ate a suspicious meatball — is satisfying comeuppance comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What was that?

dialogue.speaker: Shelley
dialogue.line: A banshee.

jokes.text: Shelley leaves, thanks Frank for the goggles.
jokes.setup: The dinner has ended in disaster.
jokes.punchline: Shelley's sincere 'Thanks for the goggles, Frank' as a parting shot — after the whole attempted boiling-oil setup — is a perfect anticlimactic beat. He's genuinely grateful for eye protection from an attack that never came.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the dinner sequence. 'Thanks for the goggles, Frank' acknowledges the gift while completely ignoring the malicious intent, and the goggles are now a souvenir of a failed assassination attempt. The economy is extraordinary — four words close out the entire subplot. High rewatch value because on second viewing you know exactly why Frank gave the goggles.

jokes.text: Dennis confronts Frank: 'I'm talking about the turd soup, man... Not eat a poopy.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dennis debrief the failed dinner scheme. Frank focuses on Charlie leaving.
jokes.punchline: Dennis cuts through the emotional conversation to the essential issue: 'You put a turd in your mouth.' His childlike 'Not eat a poopy' is the punchline — Dennis reduced to baby-talk in his disbelief.
jokes.explanation: 'Not eat a poopy' is a legitimately great comedy line — the regression to childlike language captures Dennis's bewilderment that Frank would go this far. 'Not eat a poopy' has standalone quotability outside the context of the scene. Frank's defense — 'He had me up against the wall' — implies the wall meant 'eat a turd.'

jokes.text: Dee in the bog: 'Clementine? Valentine? Diana? Denise? Dennis? Dane? Goddamn it.' She's been cycling through names for a while.
jokes.setup: Dee has been trying to remember the Waitress's name to get rescued from the bog.
jokes.punchline: The name list has escalated to include 'Dennis' and 'Dane' — Dee is now naming her own family members, having lost any tether to reasonable female names.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Dee's name attempts to include 'Dennis' and 'Dane' — clearly she has drifted off any plausible track — is a good structural joke. 'Named every name in the entire world' is an effective exaggeration.

jokes.text: Waitress: 'Oh, no, no. You got it a while back. It's just... I'm really enjoying watching you struggle.' [callback to joke #41, now with Dee visibly sinking further]
jokes.setup: Dee has been naming every possible name. The Waitress reveals she already said the right name.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress is letting Dee sink in a bog, possibly to death, purely for her own entertainment. This beat reinforces the revelation from joke #41.
jokes.explanation: The second delivery of this line lands even harder because now we see the full picture — Dee has been sinking longer, naming increasingly absurd names, while the Waitress watches with satisfaction. The sadism is complete and the structure is excellent. The Waitress calling Dee a 'drunk bitch' is the mirror image of Dee's earlier insult.

jokes.text: The Waitress attempts to save Dee, falls into the bog herself, and gets stuck. 'Oh, no, I'm not gonna do that 'cause I got a date, but I'll come back.'
jokes.setup: The Waitress finally decides to save Dee, grabs her hand, and they struggle.
jokes.punchline: The Waitress gets stuck in the bog herself — then, upon getting her legs free, leaves Dee stuck and goes to her date, promising to come back.
jokes.explanation: The escalation is excellent: Waitress gets stuck, then, once free, decides the date is more important than the woman sinking in a bog. 'I got a date, but I'll come back' is ruthlessly funny — the 'but I'll come back' is hollow reassurance delivered with complete sincerity. The echo of Dee's earlier date-desire (which the Waitress is now prioritizing over Dee's life) adds an additional ironic layer.

jokes.text: Dee, left alone sinking in the bog: 'Oh, you dirty bitch. I'm gonna get out, I'm gonna kill you.'
jokes.setup: The Waitress has abandoned Dee in the bog to go on her date.
jokes.punchline: Dee's 'I'm gonna kill you' threat from someone who is literally sinking is an impotent but totally in-character Dee response.
jokes.explanation: A functional button on the bog sequence. 'Dirty bitch' paired with 'I'm gonna kill you' while actively drowning is Dee in a nutshell — refusing to admit helplessness. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Shelley: 'A true Kelly always puts things right with the men in his life.' Beat. 'Not so much the women. Thus, the curse of the banshees.'
jokes.setup: Charlie apologizes for Frank's behavior. Shelley offers wisdom.
jokes.punchline: 'Not so much the women. Thus, the curse of the banshees.' — Shelley ties the folklore callback (banshees = wronged women) to the Kelly family pattern of ignoring women's feelings with complete nonchalance.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured callback. The whole Kelly mythology about banshees being wronged women thrown from cliffs is now crystallized into 'not so much the women — thus, the curse of the banshees.' The deadpan linking of cause and effect — ignoring women creates literal supernatural horror — is elegant dark comedy. High economy and structure. The word 'thus' is doing tremendous work, lending it the gravity of a formal theorem.

jokes.text: Mac and Shelley see a figure in the distance — Dee, covered in bog filth, shrieking and staggering — and believe she is an actual banshee. 'What was that?' 'A banshee.'
jokes.setup: The banshee folklore has been established. Dee is in the bog, covered in filth, shrieking.
jokes.punchline: The payoff of the entire episode's structural joke: Dee, in her current state, is indistinguishable from a banshee. Mac and Shelley see her and immediately conclude 'A banshee' — no elaboration, complete conviction.
jokes.explanation: This is the structural crown jewel of the episode and arguably the best payoff. The setup goes back to the priest's banshee description ('a gruesome woman covered in filth with long, stringy hair, who's horribly shrieking in the night'), which was itself an exact description of Dee in the bog — an ironic prophecy fulfilled in real time. Mac and Shelley see the shrieking filth-covered woman and say simply 'A banshee.' It earns its reaction because the setup was patient and the visual confirmation is complete. This is what structural comedy looks like: a joke planted at minute 6, paid off at minute 21, with every Dee-in-the-bog scene in between serving as silent confirmation. The economy of 'A banshee.' — two words closing an entire episode's worth of scaffolding — is extraordinary.

tmdb_overview: Mac spends a day at the seminary to truly understand what it takes to become a priest. Dennis and Frank plan an elaborate trap to humiliate Charlie's pen pal. Dee prepares for a date with an Irish doctor. Charlie bonds with his pen pal.
